item.title: John Goerzen: The Large Project Bias of CVEs
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: That turns out to be pretty difficult for a small independent project.Large projects have a way to self-assign CVE IDs. They are their own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA). There is a massive list of CNAs. Just looking at the first page of results, I see everyone from Airbus to 9front (the niche Plan 9 OS). The OpenKermit project is not a CNA.If you’re a CNA, you can create and publish CVEs on your schedule. There is apparently no external review process. You can wait for months, or publish immediately.If you’re not a CNA, you have to find someone that is. The general ones that are CNAs appear to be Github and MITRE.It’s been a week and a half and no sign of a review yet. Apparently the real review time is more than a month.The other option for projects without a CNA is via MITRE. You have to use a strange and often broken web form, logging in with either Google or Gitlab. (It seems to be broken on Firefox). Then you submit your request and wait.The first CVE I obtained for C-Kermit was CVE-2025-68920. At the time, I had not yet started the OpenKermit project. That issue was found and fixed in the context of my work maintaining C-Kermit for Debian, and Debian is a CNA.These were discovered while wearing my “upstream C-Kermit maintainer” hat. I’m sure I could ask Debian for CVEs again, but that seems a bit cheating; not everyone that maintains a FLOSS project will have connections with a distro like I do.There are a lot of components of a modern OS and Internet ecosystem that are small projects without a large institution behind them.This bias towards large organizations when it comes to communicating security problems benefits nobody. It doesn’t benefit users, and only serves to discourage timely communication. Not everyone is as persistent as I am, and when it is made so difficult to make announcements — which seem to go into a giant black hole — it’s easy to say, “why bother?”By Microsoft’s own admission, they are under-funding their CVE process on Github (which may also be poorly-designed). They blame it on increasing load due to LLMs — a problem they helped create and predicted! Having a fiction about being able to communicate a security issue in a reasonable time is worse than not offering the path at all.Linux was once a student’s experiment. Let’s not pretend that quality only matters from large projects.

item.content:encoded: A thing that really annoys me about English idiom is that when people name the four cardinal directions, they tend to say "east and west" rather than "west and east" – but they tend to say "left and right" rather than "right and left". And (in the usual north-at-the-top map orientation) those are opposite ways round.I've always struggled to tell east from west. Whenever I have to translate a spoken direction into something on a map, or vice versa, I always have to stop and think twice to make sure I haven't got them backwards. I have some mnemonics, like "west rhymes with left", or mentally zooming the map out until I can see America and Russia (and I know which of _those_ is "the West"), but they're not instantaneous, and I always have to slow down to check them.I'm convinced that this reversal in the default speech order is the reason. If my whole life I'd heard "west/east" and "left/right", I would have had no trouble matching up the one that comes first in both forms.It especially annoys me when _I_ name the directions in those orders. After I've decided it's wrong and bad, you'd think I ought at least to be able to shake the habit myself! But I said 'east, west' again this morning without thinking and kicked myself.

Vasudev Kamath: Experiment: Debian Cloud/VM Images using mkosi
item.author: copyninja
item.content:encoded: Debian's Cloud Images for various public cloud platforms and VM environments are built using a tool called debian-cloud-images, an in-house utility developed and maintained by the .The tooling uses FAI (Fully Automatic Installation) to create custom VM images for public clouds like , , and , along with the class. I wanted to convert this into a fully declarative, mkosi-based image build where the entire image is described using INI-format configuration files, with only a few post-installation scripts to handle final customizations.I've been working with various image customization formats for a long time. In my previous company, I used to build customized industrial PC distributions based purely on Debian using and a bunch of shell scripts to stitch together raw image creation, bootloader installation, etc. I've also done custom installs using on my own laptop with as the bootloader, but that was mostly hand-crafted and not automated. Once I came across , I was impressed by how a single utility can do everything and churn out a fully usable image without extra glue scripts for partitioning and image creation. You still need a few scripts to finalize some parts of the installation (via postinst hooks), but those are very minimal.So I decided: why not convert into mkosi's declarative format with a few architectural changes? My requirements were:Btrfs as the root filesystem: Partly because I like it, but primarily for the ability to use transparent compression (), subvolumes, and snapshots for atomic rollbacks when things go wrong.systemd-boot and Unified Kernel Images (UKI): Primarily because is clean and minimal—exactly what a modern bootloader should be. Combining it with UKIs and UEFI Secure Boot is bliss compared to the complexity of the GRUB2 world.This intentionally drops legacy BIOS (MBR/CSM) partitioning support in favor of pure UEFI. Modern cloud platforms (AWS Nitro, Azure Gen2, GCP) support UEFI natively, and dropping BIOS allows shedding significant legacy bootloader baggage—though it does make these images unsuitable for older, non-UEFI hypervisors.Of course, the initial heavy lifting was done mostly using Antigravity (), along with debugging, tuning, and cleanup from my side. I pointed to a local copy of and laid out my requirements: preserve parity with the original packages and configurations, while enabling selective builds for each cloud via modular profiles. The resulting specification is documented here.The repository also includes a verification script that audits functional parity against official images produced by (verifying packages, APT deb822 sources, and systemd services, while accounting for the switch to Btrfs and systemd-boot). Initial verification was performed for all Trixie profiles, and the parity report is published here.I've also booted the profile image under UEFI in a local VM to verify live bootability, , network connectivity, and APT repository setup. This completes Phase 1 of the implementation. The remaining phases outlined in the specification include:Phase 2: Immutable Images with dm-verity: Configure in systemd-repart's . Enable mkosi auto-signing for the verity root hash and pass the root hash into UKI kernel command lines automatically.Phase 3: Secure Boot & Signed UKIs: Integrate with custom owner keys or using Microsoft Third-Party CA signed shim binaries.Phase 4: System Extensions (systemd-sysext): Decouple cloud vendor agents (AWS CLI, Azure waagent, GCP guest agent) into separate system extensions. Maintain a single unified, signed base OS image across all cloud platforms.Phase 5: Btrfs Automated Rollbacks: Combine Btrfs with systemd-boot snapshot boot entries for fail-safe OS upgrades.Another advantage of this setup is that the same tooling can build images for physical laptops and bare-metal servers. For example, in an earlier post, I walked through live-booting with and manually configuring for a custom UEFI installation. With , I can simply generate a customized image locally with UKIs ready to go, live-boot the target machine, and write the image directly to the root disk.This experiment is an exploration of the power of ; I haven't discussed adoption with the yet. For now, this will continue as my pet project. While I won't be hosting pre-built binary images, anyone interested is welcome to clone the repository and build the images locally.I will probably take some more time before tackling dm-verity images, as I want to understand the nuances thoroughly before experimenting with them. Until then, happy hacking! Please report any issues or suggestions on GitHub.

item.title: Amin Bandali: EmacsConf 2026 community panel - my comments
item.author: Amin Bandali
item.content:encoded: This is a recollection of my comments from the EmacsConf 2026 community panel recording session this past weekend, where the panellists took turns answering the proposed questions, one minute per question per panellist.In addition to the live Q&A session planned for Saturday 12 December 2026 during EmacsConf 2026, all Emacs users and community members are invited to share their thoughts on the panel questions or other questions before or after the conference.1. What made you start using Emacs, and what kept you using it?I started using Emacs during my bachelor's studies. I actually learned about Vim first and was a Vim user, but I'd always found the configuration language (VimScript) a little bit clunky. Not long after, I discovered Emacs, and really loved reading and writing Emacs Lisp, so I stuck around.In addition to reading and writing Elisp being fun and enjoyable for me, I love that Emacs has been a practical embodiment of software freedom, and I'm really fond of its surrounding culture of sharing freely. There's a lot to love and appreciate about Emacs, but as a practical personal example, I've been grateful for its excellent support for bidirectional text editing. It has empowered me to read and write in Persian, my mother tongue, with ease. (Persian has a right-to-left alphabet, like Arabic and Hebrew.)2. What took you from using Emacs to actively contributing to the community - participating in forums, writing Elisp, organizing meetups, answering questions?As I continued experimenting and writing bits and pieces of Elisp to scratch my own itches, I felt compelled to share them freely as a way of giving back to the community that gave me so much.For me, the community and the people that make it up are the main deal. Emacs wouldn't be where it is and what it is today without its people, so besides programming contributions, I've tried to contribute in that area as well, for instance by reviving EmacsConf with Sacha Chua back in 2019.3. How does Emacs show up for you in real life - colleagues, meetups, friends? How did those connections form?I don't physically have people near me who use Emacs, but I've connected with many folks in our online communities, often starting with an email or IRC message. Some of those relationships started as acquaintanceship and were developed into true friendship over time, and I'm grateful to have had those friends with me.4. If you know other software communities, what's one thing Emacs could learn from them?I would encourage Emacs, our community, to focus on the people. We're living in particularly difficult times, with various kinds of hardships and uncertainty in our lives. Let's strive to treat each other with kindness, empathy, and mindfulness as we continue working together.There are great examples of other free software communities whose members have banded together and are strengthening each other and their community, as well as cautionary ones where community members have been tiring and driving out their fellow members. We could learn valuable lessons from both in how to take care of our people and ourselves.5. What's one concrete thing you wish existed in the Emacs community a year from now?I echoed the sentiments of my fellow panellists Prot and Til about doing more of the same in terms of continuing to uphold the standards of excellence and perseverance. Also, drawing inspiration from what bashbunni said, to lower the barriers of entry for people, for example through organizing different kinds of events, and experimenting with ways to make people's lengthy, elaborate Emacs configurations more tangible and accessible to others, to share various workflows and demonstrate what's possible with Emacs.I look forward to your thoughts on these and other community-related questions.Take care, and so long for now.

item.content:encoded: I ran the following benchmarks on an , a Zen 4c CPU, rented from Scaleway, running at 2.4 GHz with CPU boost disabled. I compiled the kernels with GCC 10.2: this version can compile older kernels as well as the current ones.Performance evolution of IPv6 route lookups. Versions with an asterisk have SRSO mitigation disabled.a recent full view with about 260,000 prefixes,a full view from 2017 with about 40,000 prefixes,a set of 40,000 /48 prefixes, such that 2 lookups out of 3 match, anda set of 40,000 random /128 prefixes, such that 1 lookup out of 400 matches.The major 200 ns regression introduced in Linux wiped out all these improvements. This version implements a mitigation for "Speculative Return Stack Overflow," a vulnerability affecting AMD processors, in commit fb3bd914b3ec. This mitigation adds about 20 cycles on each function return. It was backported to older kernels (5.10, 5.15, 6.1, and 6.4). To keep the results legible, I disabled the mitigation for these versions with on the kernel command-line.You can check the vulnerabilities impacting your CPU and their mitigations with . Some mitigations may depend on the microcode or on the firmware.lscpugrepPerformance evolution of IPv4 route lookups. Versions with an asterisk have SRSO mitigation disabled.I tested three scenarios:a recent full view with more than 1,000,000 prefixes,a subset of a full view from 2017 with 500,000 prefixes, anda set of 500,000 contiguous /32 prefixes.The 30 ns impact of the mitigation for in Linux is smaller than for IPv6 because IPv4 route lookups traverse fewer functions: around 4 function calls for IPv4 compared to 25 for IPv6.In Linux , I introduced a regression in commit c0c5a60f0f13 after fixing the behavior of net.ipv4.conf.all.ignore_routes_with_linkdown! item.title: Birger Schacht: Using incus for throw away VMs
item.author: Birger Schacht
item.content:encoded: For some time now I’ve been looking for a way of keeping projects I’m working on in a separate VM without much setup. There are numerous solutions to do this kind of thing using namespaces (various container technologies, firejail, flatpak, bubblewrap, …) but I wanted something that uses real virtualization. I recently stumbled upon incus and it seemed like it could be a solution to my problem. Incus is a manager for both containers and virtual machines. It is possible to create VM images that can be used as templates, meaning that other machines can then be based on them on creation. Virtual machines can be configured using “profiles”.For my use case, I have created a profile that defines how my template image should look like. In this profile I use cloud-init to configure the template machine on startup:and I use a script to regenerate the template image when I want to adapt the config:This script uses the image together with my profile to set up a machine, configure it using and store the result as an image called .To use this setup, I created a small python tool called inker that talks to the incus REST API. Using creates a new VM based on my template. Using attaches the current working directory to a VM as a readonly mount. It is possible to combine those commands like inker create | inker attach to do those two steps in one command. logs into the VM that has the current directory attached. This way I can create VMs that are connected to directories on my filesystem.I am currently playing around with this setup, but I think this could help me to have a throwaway development machine, similar to dev containers. I’m not sure yet how happy I am with , though. I was also looking at systemd-vmspawn, but there are still some features missing that I would need. But I might rewrite at some point to use a different backend.

item.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: prrd 0.1.0 at CRAN: Now With Real Concurrency
item.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
item.content:encoded: A new release of prrd arrived at CRAN today, and has already been built for r2u and on r-universe. The prrd package facilitates the parallel running [of] reverse dependency [checks] when preparing R packages. It is used extensively for releases I make of Rcpp, RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen, BH, and others.The key idea of prrd is simple, and described in some more detail on its webpage and its GitHub repo. Reverse dependency checks are an important part of package development that is easily done in a (serial) loop. But these checks are also generally as there is no or little interdependency between them (besides maybe shared build depedencies). See the (somewhat dated) screenshot (running six parallel workers, arranged in a split byobu session).This release updates internals to allow for greater concurrency. SQLite is used as the backend, both for the job queue (managed via the liteq package) as well as for storing actual reverse-dependency test results. It is well-known that SQLite copes quite well with multiple . Multiple concurrent are more challenging. We tended to get by via pragma use, but still get occassional issue even at a somewhat moderate concurrency levels. After some back and forth and trying a few approaches, more recently we established one first solution relying on very explicity (OS-level, filesystem-based) locking via package filelock. That worked.We mentioned this in an old issue that had circled around the same question with a number of posts over the years, but no resolution. This comment seemingly awoke Gábor, and he nailed this years-open issue with a fine pull request deploying and well as a loop around to not immediately fail. I borrowed/ported that approach to prrd and we now have a second solution (and no longer need filelock). On a somewhat better server with enough cores and memory, I am now running eighteen concurrent workers—watched via three multi-pane byobu windows. Works like a charm without issues. At last! A big thanks to Gábor for finding another solution, and especially that only relies on SQLite.The release is summarised in the NEWS entry:Changes in prrd version 0.1.0 (2026-11-07)Concurrent operations are now supported via updated sqlite semantics borrowed with appreciation from This follows an interim solution relying on use; however this later package is not needed so no increase in dependencies

item.title: Mike Gabriel: OpenAGPS - The New Kid on the Block
item.author: sunweaver
item.content:encoded: There is a new project coming to Open Source Software land these days: OpenAGPS. It is not yet 100% functional, but we are working on it. It is not fully operational, yet, but we are on it.Let me introduce OpenAGPS to you...The domain of assisted geo location services has been left to a few big tech providers. When using GPS on mobile devices, most of us send info on our approximate device location (based on cell tower IDs seen by our devices around us) mostly to Google's SUPL service in order to facilitate a faster GNSS/GPS lock on the satellites flying above us.Without assistance, retrieving a GNSS/GPS lock on sufficient satellites includes "finding" those satellites and once found retrieving data (in bytes/sec) from them. In some regions, this leads to waiting periods of up to 45 minutes, before a mobile devices has gained a lock on sufficient satellites (3 or more).In Assisted-GNSS/GPS, "other" information (such as cell tower IDs) gets used to estimate what GNSS/GPS satellites are currently passing over one's location. With AGPS, the mobile devices retrieve information via a so-called SUPL server, containing two details: a list of potential satellites above and their dataframes. Esp. providing those dataframes over the device's internet connection (and not via the GNSS/GPS receiver downloading it from the satellite itself) speeds up the lock-on process of the mobile tremendously (several seconds to a few minutes).However, for this mechanism to work, your device will share your IMSI (although not needed for AGPS), a list of cell towers around you and their signal strengths with the provider of the SUPL service, revealing your approximate position. In total, this allows SUPL providers to re-identify each mobile device and create motion profiles of each such device (and its owner). If the SUPL service is hosted by one main provider (i.e. Google SUPL), there is a lot of valuable information available to them for free that they can commercialize.Currently, there is only one mitigation method available to hide one's location info from the SUPL server(s) at e.g. Google: using a SUPL proxy server implementation (available as OSS, provided by and used in e.g. GrapheneOS). A SUPL proxy still depends on the big tech service provider(s) for SUPL as it merely proxies SUPL requests from mobile devices through to the proprietary SUPL services, at e.g. Google, but the mobile device is being camouflaged behind the SUPL proxy in use.OpenAGPS, on the contrary, will be a fully independent implementation from proprietary service providers, and it will refrain from collecting and commercializing end users’ data. It will be driven by individuals of the OpenAGPS community. There will likely be one central service that the OpenAGPS project plans to host and operate (the Porygon frontend/backend, OpenAGPS's GNSS Almanach service), but except from that SUPL servers can be self-hosted by individuals, companys or other communities. The requesting mobile devices' IDs will be hidden from the Porygon server (like with existing SUPL proxy implementations), so that the only centrally operated component (the Porygon Almanach server) does not know who is requesting what geo position information (and thus cannot collect such data, neither derive info about where requesting devices are located).In addition, with a large OpenAGPS community, it is imaginable (in theory) that there will also be multiple central Almanach servers available on the internet (with parallel networks of base stations attached to each GNSS Almanach server).Collecting Satellite DataThe OpenAGPS project is not simply a software that admins/users can install, it needs kind of a huge and global community to operate/host/house its base station network.The challenge with providing a community-driven AGPS service on the internet is that up-to-date (real-time!) GNSS/GPS satellite position data is not available for free download. Almanach data can be obtained per region from various organisations, but then their datasets are often days to weeks old, thus too outdated. GNSS/GPS satellites are not geo-stationary, they circulate around the planet. Their position is dependent on the current date-time. A globally spanning network of GNSS/GPS base stations will do the trick here. We will need a community that harvests the needed satellite data in real time and makes it available through the Porygon Almanach server to all OpenAGPS users.The OpenAGPS project will depend on at least one community member every ~40-50 km² to operate a so-called OpenAGPS base station: These base stations are stationary, need to run 24/7, and they will harvest GNSS/GPS statellite data information from the satellites above in real-time and share this data with the (central) Porygon server, continuously. The Porygon server will create a timestamp-dependent "map" of all seen satellites and extrapolate locations between base stations' Almanach data updates.Help making OpenAGPS a Success: Host a Base StationTo make OpenAGPS a success, we need volunteers who are willing to host (actually: house) an OpenAGPS base station at their home or work place (or both). Users will only be able to use their self-hosted OpenAGPS SUPL server with their mobile devices (instead of e.g. Google SUPL), if we manage to establish sufficient coverage with those base stations in the area of interest, so that the OpenAGPS Almanach will get populated with sufficient satellite position data.Support this project by Co-Funding itIf you realize that you have an interest in this project and would like to improve your level of digital sovereignty in your government, organization, at your home, etc. then consider sending financial support to the project. If you want to support us, please get in touch with Raoul Kramer at BetaBreak or Mike Gabriel at Fre(i)e Software GmbH. If you are a software developer and would like to contribute to OpenAGPS, also get in touch and let us meet at FOSDEM 2027.A huge thanks to the NLnet Foundation for funding this project's bootstrap phase. Follow-up funding has been applied for, so please keep fingers crossed!

item.title: Isoken Ibizugbe: Seeing Accessibility in Debian
item.author: Isoken Ibizugbe
item.content:encoded: Recently, I’ve been noticing something on packaging around my house that I used to glance right past: raised Braille dots on a carton of medicine, and embossed markings on a container of body cream. I’ve always known what Braille looked like, but I never paid close attention to it. Now that I’m actively working on accessibility testing for the Debian Installer, I see it everywhere.It made me reflect on how accessibility usually enters our consciousness. In tech, we’re taught about accessibility as a best practice when designing user interfaces or web apps. But realistically, you mostly see it implemented well in massive global software, like mobile operating systems or browsers like Firefox. You rarely see accessibility features integrated into local Nigerian physical products or everyday tech. Paying attention to these details made me realize how much care goes into making sure every person is considered, and how vital that mindset really is.Manual Testing & The openQA BottleneckMy recent work with Debian has been focused on automating tests for the Debian Installer’s accessibility features, specifically validating Braille display emulation.I started out by manually testing following the official steps on the Debian Installer Accessibility Wiki. Once I understood the manual flow, the next goal was figuring out how to automate it inside openQA.Initially, the idea was to initialize from the bootloader by adding parameters to the Grub (GRUB=”brltty=auto”)and it should start the installation with the braille visual. However, this didn’t work, the parameters never initiated the brttyl and it was a huge blocker going back and forth. Getting brltty to talk to the test runner in that environment would have required sweeping changes across the main Debian openQA instance configuration.Instead of pushing for complex system-wide changes on the instance, we started looking for easier alternative approaches and noted the complicated ones, when we advance in the test.We brainstormed streaming the display output directly to a dedicated file to capture and verify the Braille virtual display output. Ultimately, nested virtualization proved to be the most easiest path forward. You can check out the implementation details and changes in the Merge RequestAs part of this work, I joined the debian-accessibility mailing list to introduce what we were building and share our progress.The responses were encouraging. I got some feedback and suggestions and the thread also created a discussion on how accessible the installation process currently feels for blind or visually impaired users, and where they also find issues. It served as a great reminder that test suites aren’t just about passing CI checks, they’re about serving actual people who rely on these systems every day.

Vincent Bernat: Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
item.author: Vincent Bernat
item.content:encoded: I disable logging to avoid collecting personal information. While the bunny.net GDPR page promises they anonymize data, it is unclear what CloudFront keeps in its own logs when logging is disabled.The only downside of the offering is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their support: two minutes later, they answered they are working on it but have no to share.I run seven small NixOS virtual machines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Sydney. Bunny's scriptable DNS lets me return the IP addresses of the . The browser falls back to the second server if the first one is down.The above script relies on the RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper, which returns the closest alive server to the user. Thanks to Doggo, we can check it works as expected, at least for :doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch The most annoying drawback of this method is that a user from Buenos Aires gets both São Paulo (1000 mi, 30 ms ) and Ashburn (5200 mi, 140 ms ). Most resolvers randomize the order, so the user may pull the web page from Ashburn. We could return only the nearest server—and swap the scripted record with the built-in geographic routing instead. But if the server becomes unavailable, the browser has no alternative until the DNS cache expires. It leaves a short window of unavailability, even with a short .The HTTPS record solutionThe HTTPS DNS record, defined in RFC 9460, solves both the availability and the latency issues. Modern browsers query this record to get additional information to reach an HTTP server, including an alternative port and the application layer protocol—HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. Each record has a priority. We can ask browsers to contact the nearest server first and fall back to the next one if the first is unavailable:This looks like the ideal solution! Unfortunately, Chrome ignores any record whose target is not , hence the last record at priority 3. Moreover, unlike with a , Bunny DNS does not return the IP addresses for and in the additional section. The resolver needs to send a first request to get the record, and a second to resolve .HTTPS records are still too new for this use case. Back to the drawing board! 📐As a compromise, the script returns the two nearest servers if they are at a similar distance from the user. Otherwise, it returns only the nearest one with a lower of 2 minutes.We can check it with . From Chicago, we get only the Ashburn server with a of 2 minutes, while from Mexico, we get both Ashburn and San Jose.doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch doggo--reverse.161.44.145.28.219.155 The complete code is a bit more complex. It works around RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() supporting only IPv4, and it handles the case where there are not enough alive servers to build an answer.Route 53 covered one additional use case of mine: serving to solve DNS-01 ACME challenges. Unlike Route 53, Bunny DNS cannot restrict access to a single zone with a fine-grained access policy. As this usage requires neither high availability nor low latency, I replaced Route 53 with Hickory, a memory-safe DNS server written in Rust. It supports automatic DNSSEC signatures and dynamic updates. Its configuration is simple:The provided zone file only seeds the database on first start. I delegate DNS-01 challenges to this zone with records:Unfortunately, Bunny DNS cannot publish a record in a zone. I need one to secure the zone and certificate delivery. Therefore, I host the zone on deSEC, a free DNS hosting service run by a non-profit organization based in Berlin. I derive the record to publish in from the record of :acme.luffy.cx dig@nsupdate.luffy.cxDNSKEY+noall+answerdnssec-dsfromkey-aSHA-256-f-Overall, I am quite happy with the switch to . There are still a few rough edges, like the inability to publish records, the lack of HTTP/3, and the IPv4-only RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper. The bill went from US$5 per month to US$1. So far, performance is on par with AWS, but I only finalized the current setup, including the server in Sydney, in late October. I need a bit more time to gather more data, and I'll post a short update. 📈

John Goerzen: Letter from a Kansan: “Would You Rather Be Right or Happy?”
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: As a person that has lived in Kansas almost all my life, I have never seen such good political news for this state as we got this week. It is a stunning rebuke of fascism from across the country.One of the many pieces of wisdom from mechanic Tom Magliozzi is this question: “Would you rather be right, or happy?” He often asked it in the context of somebody that had just won an argument.This is my plea to all our progressive friends: remember that question, and keep it in mind carefully over the next 2 years. We can either build on this momentum for an even bigger victory in 2028, or we can start to lose this unique coalition.Kansans spend our lives being misunderstood and forgotten.Many of us, myself included, visit large cities regularly.It is a more surprising event when someone from a large city drives down one of our dirt roads. The kind of road that leaves your car covered in mud when you drive your daughter to school. The kind of road that we drive on for 3 miles before we reach the nearest paved road.Statisticians label Topeka, the capital of Kansas and city of 126,000 people, as rural.The nearst town to me, 7 miles away, has a population of 600. In winter, many people here still leave their keys in their running, unlocked cars while they run into the grocery store. The person at the bank, the owner of the grocery store, the mechanic, the electricians, the builders, the people that run the local museum, all know my name and recognize me. Not because I’m famous locally, but because this is normal here. We are a community, a real one.Yet I’ve lost long-time friends, especially from the west coast, because, while I’m progressive, I still talk to Republicans. They thought Republicans are so evil, they ought to be shunned and ostracized.It probably doesn’t compute to a San Franciscan what it means to live in a county that went 80% for Trump one time. A county of about 10,000 people living in a space larger than Los Angeles, New York, and San Jose — combined. (Those cities have a combined population of about 13 million, living on the same amount of land as 10,000 people do out here.)If I avoided talking to Republicans, it wouldn’t be them that would be isolated. It would be me.Out here, many of us have lived with each other for generations. We may go on living with them for generations. If somebody’s car is stuck in the mud, the first person that comes by with a truck and a rope will probably pull them out. Nobody asks who you voted for. This is what you do for neighbors, because neighbors are humans, and next time it might be me that’s stuck in the mud.I can be as incensed as anyone else about what the fascists are doing. I don’t have direct knowledge of how a lot of people vote. But I take a deep breath sometimes and remind myself: these are my neighbors. I’ve seen them go out of their way to be kind and generous with all walks of humanity. (Yes, even whatever groups you’re imaginging to argue with me about.)This is part of how Adam Hamilton defeated Roger Marshal. The anti-Trump sentiment wasn’t enough on its own. Lifelong Republicans dissatisfied with how Trump handled things weren’t just going to vote for any Democrat. They needed someone that was safe. Someone that talked to them as humans. Someone that respected them.Adam Hamilton went and shook hands with MAGA protestors at his events. He told them “I want to be your senator, too.”I have already been seeing some progressives say things like, “Don’t cut them any slack. Remember how many times people voted for fascism! They need to still be ostracized.”That, folks, is the way we lose. It is the wrong strategy everywhere. And it is especially culturally wrong in the close-knit communities — again, actual communities where people know each other and have for years — that make up the heartland.Building relationships with people different than us is our best chance to build on this coalition. And, isn’t that what progressive values call for?So, celebrate this victory. Clap for all the activists that made it happen.And, before you set off to alienate your new and tentative allies, ask yourself:“Would I rather be right? Or win again?”

item.title: Juan Manuel Méndez Rey: Hello, Planet Debian
item.author: Juan Manuel Méndez Rey
item.content:encoded: Hello, Planet Debian. My blog was added to the Planet today, so I think the polite thing is to introduce myself before you start finding my posts between yours.I am Juan Manuel Méndez Rey, from Sevilla. In Debian I am mendezr, and on OFTC I am Vejeta. I have been using Linux since 1994 and Debian since 1998. For a long time that was all: a happy user, installing, breaking things, reading the mailing lists from the outside. I started contributing in October 2025, and last month I became a Debian Maintainer.The way in was a friend. Back in 2019 Arturo Borrero Gonzalez filed RFP #943703 for Stremio, and for years he kept telling me I should pick it up. In September 2025 I finally listened and turned it into an ITP. It took longer than I like to admit, but Stremio is now in Debian, and I told that story here. A six year old RFP turned out to be a very good first package.Somewhere along the way I discovered that what I enjoy most is bringing old software back.The first one came from tille, who asked for help in #debian-tinytasks with xwpe, a Borland style programming editor for the terminal that nobody was looking after. I adopted it, and then I ended up as its upstream maintainer too. I fixed the old bugs and added LSP and DAP, so now an editor from 1993 can debug Go. It ships on several distributions, in Homebrew and on the BSDs. The canonical repo is on Codeberg, and the long version is in this post.The second one is older and took much longer. Conquer is a Unix strategy game written by Ed Barlow and Adam Bryant in 1987, and I lost many hours of my youth to it. It never had a free licence. I first asked about it on debian-legal in October 2006, and I spent the next 20 years tracking down the authors, one email at a time. Today Conquer v4 and V5 are GPL-3.0. It is not packaged in Debian yet, that is the next step, but you can already play it in the browser.CEF took me six months and brought me into the Chromium team, and these days I am mostly with the syft, trivy and grype security stack and with Scala 3 and sbt for Debian.To Arturo, for the nudge. To dilinger, tille and tsimonq2, my DM advocates, for trusting me.And if you can sponsor uploads for syft, trivy, grype or the Scala work, I would be very grateful. The details are on my wiki page.

item.title: John Goerzen: Must we always use LLMs this way?
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: Just because most people hold AI a certain way, doesn’t mean that we always must, either now or in the future.As I noted in that piece, and my shades of gray post, I am well aware — — the notion that a lot of frontier AI models have disturbing ethical concerns that we shouldn’t dismiss, including concentration of power and wealth, environmental concerns, unethical scraping and training, the financial bubble they seem to be creating, and more. The most poisonous of AI cheerleaders are accelerating enshittification while cutting quality all over the place. AI slop is also a real problem, which I’ll discuss in a bit.Before I dive in, I need to mention that no AI assistance was used for writing this post, and I have been using em dashes — correctly — for years before LLMs did. Secondly, while popular discourse seems to use “AI” and “LLM” interchangeably, the AI field is much more broad and much more old than LLMs. I will, nonetheless, adopt the common “AI” jargon here, but be more specific when necessary to differentiate.The present and future of LLMs outside of the cloud-hosted frontier modelsWhat differentiates productive use of AI from slopThe two are related, in fact. Doctorow discussed how he never uses AI to write anything, but he sometimes uses it as an assistant to help him write. Is that contradictory? Not really. He gave this example: he remembered a quote from a podcast, which he wanted to cite and attribute correctly. But he couldn’t remember which podcast or who said it. So he fired up Whisper, an open-weight model you can download and run locally, even on meagre hardware. Whisper is a speech-to-text model. Doctorow ran likely podcast episodes (from the target range and set of podcasts he listens to) through the model, and at that point it was a regular search. He found the quote, then went back and listened to the episode at that time spot to verify its accuracy.It would have taken so much time to do this without Whisper that he simply would not have done it otherwise. His writing was better because of AI. Not because AI wrote any words for him, but because it helped him find the right ideas and attributions. He didn’t even have to trust its transcription; it pointed him at the right place, and then he could transcribe with precision.I too have used Whisper in much the same way. A little while back, I digitized many hours of old family audio recordings going back to the 1970s. Thanks to Whisper, which I ran locally primarily during hours of being fully solar-powered, I have a searchable index to these gems. A person I know recently asked me if I knew any way to transcribe some old family recordings he had. I told him I could run it through Whisper. It wouldn’t have great punctuation, but most of the words would be there. This meant a lot to him and his family; what I did in 2 minutes would have taken him many days (I presume he is not a fast typist as well.)So we can start by naming: AI isn’t just chatbots, and AI can help even if it isn’t writing anything.Doctorow goes on to ask the question: what happens after the AI bubble bursts? I do believe it will, as Ed Zitron has carefully documented for us for a long time now. The environmental damage done by frontier training and inference in the last few years will, of course, be done. But as he points out, we’ll be left with a plethora of surprisingly-capable open weight models, a community that has made significant strides running them on low-end devices (even phones), and a massive buildup of clean energy that hopefully will be finally able to offset some polluting energy once these heavy users drop off the grid.So then what? Will the world just throw away the likes of Whisper and Gemma? Obviously not. Doctorow imagines, credibly, a situation in which individuals and universities tinker with locally-run models, iterating on them and improving them with the more traditional scale of resources available to individuals and universities. In other words, this future sounds a lot like the earlier days of Open Source.As Ed Zitron has pointed out, the real costs of frontier AI have been hidden as these companies rack up fantastical losses. When the bubble bursts, the real costs of frontier AI are likely to be high enough that CEO’s won’t be able to ignore the poor ROI. But we’ll be left with these artifacts, these open-weight starting points, that people can use.That brings me to my central thesis: a lot of anti-AI sentiment is focused on the real downsides of the hyped uses of AI, and fails to account for the more ethical advances being made now, and likely to come in the future.Varying quality of AI useWe are all familiar with AI slop. I’ve seen it, and have an increasingly skeptical eye when I see “new” projects announced in even places as niche as a BBS community (where I see things like new terminal emulators announced, written in shockingly-poor nodejs, and such). I’ve seen documents that take many pages to say what amounts to nothing intelligble to a human, with perfect grammar. I’ve seen pull requests that have a description that amounts to several pages of slop. I’ve personally seen an AI agent do things like correctly detect passing an untrusted argument to a shell, then propose a broken quoting algorithm to fix it (rather than proper sanitization and exec() or, better yet, avoiding the call altogether.)I’ve also seen AI tools very quickly and accurately identify bugs that had passed human review, even professional security reviews, for years. I’ve seen them bring more joy to some people’s jobs by handling the more drudgery parts of the jobs. One of my favorite podcasts, Oxide and Friends, had an episode called Engineering Rigor in the LLM age and credibly described ways in which careful use of LLMs can quality and safety. Yes, I said increase. (Oxide and Friends are not hype cheerleaders by any means; these are very serious people with solid technical chops, and I know some of them.)What accounts for this disconnect?We can point to many factors, but Doctorow asks a fundamental question: who is in charge? Is it the person or the computer? Does the AI service people, or do people service the AI?In some of the most ridiculously AI-first companies, it is very clearly the latter. Mandates from CEOs to increase AI usage lead to perverse outcomes that sacrifice quality. The AI is in charge. I’ve never seen an AI be any good at design questions, and it’s no wonder than all these vibe-coded apps have the same generic feeling of crappiness.But when the AI is used pragmatically as a junior research assistant, that’s a different approach. Its output is greeted skeptically, its actions distrusted, and it’s never asked to design something. These are the cases where I’ve seen it make a meaningful difference.All this adds up to why I was opposed to the Debian proposals that would have banned LLM use. Those votes are hard to change. They would have left Debian in a vulnerable position of being unable to react to accurate security findings if they originated with an LLM, or left Debian unable to adopt ethical use of models.It would be akin to saying “you should never buy a PC because Windows 11 is terrible.” I agree Windows 11 is terrible, but saying something like that is so dismissive of all those that have invested decades of their time in building something better.So, I find AI hype to be uncredible and dangerous. I also find knee-jerk reactions to AI to be the same. They are actually a form of capitulation: they let the AI megacorps dictate the terms of the conversation to revolve around them.Case study: Debian’s DFSG scannerFor a long time, my two biggest annoyances with Debian have been the difficulty of packaging Rust and Go packages with their long dependency trees, and how long it takes a new package to get reviewed. About a year ago, the latter process was set on a path to reform, and it has gotten dramatically better. It also cuts off a potential connection with someone that hasn’t yet heard of Linux. Some people may not jump from Windows 11 (or the ChatGPTs of the world) immediately, but pretending that it’s ChatGPT or nothing does a disservice to all those that are trying to do research etchically.We should state at the outset that Debian takes compliance with the Debian Free Software Guidelines (DFSG) extremely seriously. Every new package gets a review, and these reviews often catch things that upstream repos and other distros don’t. One common example would be a package that has a stated copyright and license, but then includes files that bear a different copyright and license.You can imagine reviewing packages at this level of detail isn’t a fun task for people, and it’s hard to find volunteers to do it. Perhaps the answer to this should be “Debian should stop caring so much more than everyone else”, and perhaps you’re right (and perhaps you aren’t).In any case, the DFSG team that reviews this added what amounts to an LLM-backed license linter. Its job is to produce an initial assessment that the license statements documented in debian/copyright are correct, thorough, and in compliance with DFSG. This report was not taken to be authoritative, but was designed to help with some initial assessments.There were some predictable reactions. People were angry that the DFSG team had added this tool without any communication about it (justifiably so, I’d say). Many were angry just because of LLM. People made assumptions about what kind of model it used, what kind of quality it would produce, how definitive it would be in the project.It is worth noting here that Debian is uniquely decentralized. There is a central policy, but maintainers are free to maintain their packages how they like. They don’t have to use a standard location for a Git repo, or even use Git.One person said essentially, “it’s fine for others to use whatever tool they want, but I shouldn’t have to be exposed to LLM slop.” The other perspective boiled down to, “why should they keep the reports secret? If you want to proactively fix things, or flag false positives, why not?”As Andreas Tille wrote, “I have read the LLM reviews carefully, and in many cases their findings inspired additional commits to improve my packaging. In some cases, they even helped me catch mistakes that led me to reject an upload myself before human inspection.”Joey Hess raises an interesting risk: that LLMs will remove the incentive for Debian to actually fix its cumbersome processes, by letting an LLM paper them over. I have seen this tendency in other contexts, both at work and at home, as well. It’s a real risk, especially if Debian doesn’t tackle the packaging problem for Rust and Go.The Mastodon post that prompted me to write this began a chain of events that started with “Uploaders will be forced to address LLMs issues without human inspection.” I don’t believe that will be the case; it goes too far against the Debian ethos.I encourage everyone to take a deep breath. We are all getting used to a shifting landscape. We will all make missteps, myself included. The issues are complicated, the picture isn’t black and white, and there is incredible hype around the ecosystem that can make finding nuance difficult.Let’s be kind to each other, fellow humans.But, I do not care if you are kind to Claude.

item.title: Vasudev Kamath: Releasing debvulns with needrestart and kernel vulnerability handling
item.author: copyninja
item.content:encoded: After quite some time, I picked up again to implement what I mentioned in my previous post: exporting reboot required status and identifying services that need a restart. Additionally, I wanted to ensure kernel vulnerabilities are not marked as fixed unless the running kernel matches or exceeds the fixed version. Both features are now live in version (intermediate release only included the needrestart functionality).When you update packages on a system, security fixes do not take effect until running processes actually use the updated binaries from disk. When an upgrade occurs, existing processes continue executing the older, vulnerable code loaded into memory, while only newly spawned instances pick up the fixed binary. The package in Debian exists specifically for this purpose. It can run in either report mode or action mode: report mode provides machine-readable output, while action mode automatically restarts affected services.Why integrate needrestart into debvulns? is a standalone utility that can run independently or hook into to run automatically after an upgrade. On desktop systems, it typically runs interactively with a TUI prompt; on headless servers, it can be set to take non-interactive default actions. In batch mode, it avoids restarting sensitive system components (such as ) to prevent destabilizing the session.Integrating this into is not about replacing or , but rather bringing vulnerability and remediation state into a single, discoverable interface. aggregates these signals into a standard format—in this case, Prometheus metrics and tags that can be visualized in Grafana, monitored by alerting systems, or consumed downstream by automation tools.Why Special Handling for Kernel?Just as user-space daemons require a restart after patching, a patched kernel requires a system reboot into the new image before the vulnerability is truly mitigated. Previously, only verified whether the patched package version was installed on disk. If the deb package was installed, the CVE was marked as resolved, which creates a false sense of security while running the old kernel.With this release, now checks the active running kernel release. A kernel vulnerability is considered resolved only when the system is running the fixed kernel version. Until a reboot happens, the system remains reported as vulnerable.The updated dashboard reflects these changes below. It will need further polish, but key metrics and restart/reboot states are now visible:These were the two pending functional areas I wanted to cover, and no further major features are planned for now. Next up will be reviewing the entire codebase to identify potential optimizations and remove any unnecessary complexity. I haven't done a full pass through the repository since the initial skeleton implementation, so testing edge cases and cleaning up the internals will be the main focus. This will likely take some time since I only hack on this during weekend downtime. Until then, happy hacking, give the new release a try, and file an issue if you run into bugs.

item.title: Vincent Bernat: Network lab with QEMU
item.author: Vincent Bernat
item.content:encoded:
To experiment with network stuff, I was using -based network labs. Many alternatives exist, like GNS3, Netkit, Marionnet or Cloonix. All of them are great viable solutions but I still prefer to stick to my minimal home-made solution with virtual machines. Here is why:I didn’t want to use . They take a lot of space and they have to be maintained. They also become cluttered, especially if you try to reuse them across several labs. They are also difficult to share.I want to be able to access my . It contains the important configuration files related to the lab and I can put them in the right place thanks to symbolic links when the lab starts. It also makes exchanging files with the lab quite easy.I don’t want to . This allows me to be cheap on memory and each virtual system should boot in a few seconds.The use of had some drawbacks:It may be buggy. For example, it is currently not possible to use gdbserver inside without a patch. Sometimes, the kernel won’t even compile.However, features HostFS, a filesystem providing access to any part of the host filesystem. This is the killer feature which allows me to not use any virtual disk image and to get access to my home directory right from the guest.I discovered recently that QEMU provided 9P, a similar filesystem on top of VirtIO, the paravirtualized IO framework.Booting QEMU with a minimal kernelMy initial goal was to experiment with Nicolas Dichtel’s IPv6 ECMP patch. Therefore, I needed to configure a custom kernel. I have started from , removed everything that was not necessary, added what I needed for my lab (mostly network stuff) and added the appropriate options for VirtIO drivers:From here, you can start your kernel with the following command ( is the appropriate ):qemu-system-x86_64-m256m-displaynone-nodefconfig-no-user-config-nodefaults-chardevstdio,idcharserial0,signaloff-deviceisa-serial,chardevcharserial0,idserial0-chardevsocket,idcon0,path/vm--console.pipe,server,nowait-moncon0,modereadline,default-kernel-appendSince there is no disk to boot from, the kernel will panic when trying to mount the root filesystem. QEMU is configured to not display video output (). A serial port is defined and uses as a backend. The kernel is configured to use this serial port as a console (). A VirtIO console could have been used instead but it seems it is not possible to make it work early in the boot process.The QEMU monitor is setup to listen on a Unix socket. It is possible to connect to it with socat UNIX:$TMP/vm-$name-console.pipe -.I was initially unable to mount the host filesystem as the root filesystem for the guest directly by the kernel. In a comment, Josh Triplett told me to use as the mount tag to solve this problem. I keep using an in this post but the lab on GitHub has been updated to not use one.Here is how to build a small initial ramdisk: setup_initrdinfo/initrd mkdir-pcopy_execbusybox/bin/busybox applet/bin/busybox--listln-sbusybox/bin/cp/init
find.cpio--quiet-R:0-o-Hnewcgzip>/initrd.gz The function is stolen from the package in Debian. It will ensure that the appropriate libraries are also copied. Another solution would have been to use a static .The setup script is copied as in the initial ramdisk. It will detect it has been invoked as such. If it were omitted, a shell would be spawned instead. Remove the call if you want to experiment manually.The flag allows QEMU to use this initial ramdisk.Let’s mount our root filesystem using . This is quite easy. First QEMU needs to be configured to export the host filesystem to the guest:qemu-system-x86_64-fsdevlocal,security_modelpassthrough,idfsdev-root,path,readonly-devicevirtio-9p-pci,idfs-root,fsdevfsdev-root,mount_tagrootshare can either be or any directory containing a complete filesystem. Mounting it from the guest is quite easy:mkdir-p/target/ro mount-t9prootshare/target/ro-ovirtio,version9p2000.u You should find a complete root filesystem inside . I have used instead of because the latter does not allow a program to a host mount point.Now, you have a read-only root filesystem (because you do not want to mess with your existing root filesystem and moreover, you did not run this lab as root, did you?). Let’s use a union filesystem. Debian comes with AUFS while Ubuntu and OpenWRT have migrated to overlayfs. I was previously using AUFS but got errors on some specific cases. It is still not clear which one will end up in the kernel. So, let’s try .I didn’t find any patchset ready to be applied on top of my kernel tree. I was working with David Miller’s net-next tree. Here is how I have applied the patch on top of it:gitremoteaddtorvaldsgit://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux-2.6.git gitfetchtorvalds gitremoteaddoverlayfsgit://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/mszeredi/vfs.git gitfetchoverlayfs gitmerge-baseoverlayfs.v15v3.6 gitcheckout-bnet-next+overlayfs gitcherry-pick4cbe5a555fa58a79b6ecbb6c531b8bab0650778d..overlayfs.v15 Don’t forget to enable in . Here is how I configured the whole root filesystem:info mkdir/target mkdir/target/ro mkdir/target/rw mkdir/target/overlay
mount-t9prootshare/target/ro-ovirtio,version9p2000.u mount-ttmpfstmpfs/target/rw-orw mount-toverlayfsoverlayfs/target/overlay-o/target/ro,upperdir/target/rw mount-n-tprocproc/target/overlay/proc mount-n-tsysfssys/target/overlay/sys
info mount-t9phomeshare/target/overlay/root-ovirtio,version9p2000.L,access,rw
info mkdir/target/overlay/lab mount-t9plabshare/target/overlay/lab-ovirtio,version9p2000.L,access,rw
info cp/target/overlay chroot/target/overlayYou have to export your and the lab directory from host:qemu-system-x86_64-fsdevlocal,security_modelpassthrough,idfsdev-root,path,readonly-devicevirtio-9p-pci,idfs-root,fsdevfsdev-root,mount_tagrootshare-fsdevlocal,security_modelnone,idfsdev-home,path-devicevirtio-9p-pci,idfs-home,fsdevfsdev-home,mount_taghomeshare-fsdevlocal,security_modelnone,idfsdev-lab,pathdirname-devicevirtio-9p-pci,idfs-lab,fsdevfsdev-lab,mount_taglabshare You know what is missing from our network lab? Network setup. For each LAN that I will need, I spawn a VDE switch: setup_switchinfoscreen-tstart-stop-daemon--make-pidfile--pidfile--start--startasvde_switch----sockscreen-XTo attach an interface to the newly created LAN, I use:-sha1sumawk qemu-system-x86_64-netnic,modelvirtio,macaddr,vlan-netvde,sock/switch-.sock,vlanThe use of a VDE switch allows me to run the lab as a non-root user. It is possible to give Internet access to each , either by using the flag or using on a special switch. I prefer the latter solution since it will allow the VMs to speak to each other.This lab was mostly done to debug both the kernel and Quagga. Each of them can be debugged remotely.While the kernel features KGDB, its own debugger, compatible with GDB, it is easier to use the built inside QEMU.qemu-system-x86_64-gdbunix:/vm--gdb.pipe,server,nowait To connect to the remote GDB server from the host, first locate the file at the root of the source tree and run GDB on it. The kernel has to be compiled with to get the appropriate debugging symbols. Then, use with the Unix socket to attach to the remote debugger:gdbvmlinux You can now set breakpoints and resume the execution of the kernel.It is easier to debug the kernel if optimizations are not enabled. However, it is not possible to disable them globally. You can however disable them for some files. For example, to debug , add to , remove and type .To debug a program inside QEMU, you can just use as usual. Your directory is available and it should therefore be straightforward. However, if you want to perform some remote debugging, that’s quite easy. Add a new serial port to QEMU:qemu-system-x86_64-chardevsocket,idcharserial1,path/vm--serial.pipe,server,nowait-deviceisa-serial,chardevcharserial1,idserial1 Start in the guest:libtoolexecutegdbserver/dev/ttyS1zebra/zebra And from the host, you can attach to the remote process:libtoolexecutegdbzebra/zebra For a demo, have a look at the following video:

item.content:encoded: In hydrology, a is a channel that forks away from a river and flows on to the sea, the opposite of a tributary. Debian is the river much of the Linux world forks from, so for a release called forky, that is my proposal for its artwork: one river, many forks.All generated by code. A small Python program grows the river by the rules of real deltas, and renders every wallpaper, login screen, boot splash and GRUB background from it, dark and light, at any resolution: the showcase offers 51 sizes to download, from phones to 8K.It comes in eight colours, and with the palette editor you can fork your own: change any colour or option live in your browser, or roll random ones, then download the wallpaper or build the whole theme locally. item.title: Matthew Garrett: Getting Google Cast on my Soundbar
item.author: Matthew Garrett
item.content:encoded: I have a Samsung Q800A soundbar. It ships with built-in support for the Apple Airplay protocol, but I’m not really an Apple kind of guy so that’s never been particularly helpful for me. So, instead, I have a Chromecast Audio plugged into it via TOSLINK, and that works fine - except for the fact that there’s no way to explicitly pick TOSLINK as the audio input. Instead, there’s a “Digital In” option that refers to both the optical in and eARC input from a TV. Not inherently a problem, given I’m unlikely to be watching TV while listening to music, but my TV is a Samsung Frame, a device that’s intended to display art whenever someone is standing nearby, and which infuriatingly generates an eARC signal even if it’s only in art mode and isn’t going to make any noise. This switches the soundbar away from optical and I get sad. I could plug a video cast device into the HDMI port on the soundbar and cast audio to that, but then the art would get replaced with album covers whenever I’m playing music, and again that’s not quite the ambience I want. Still, none of this is that important.Until I learned that the Australian version of the soundbar have Google Cast support. The firmware image was downloadable from Samsung support, so I grabbed that, but unfortunately found that it was encrypted. However, if I downloaded the firmware image for the US model, the encrypted blob was identical - there’s no difference in the underlying firmware between the two of them. So, how come one has support, and the other doesn’t?I’d need an unencrypted copy of the firmware to have a real chance of figuring this out, and the easiest way to get one was to just run an ebay watch for a broken model of the same series. Once I had one in my hands I used hot air to remove the eMMC storage from the device, cleaned up the chip, and then stuck it in one of these adapters to read it on a local system. Samsung uses a weird in-house filesystem called VDFS4 on some of their devices and this was one of them, so I needed to cobble together a kernel that was compatible with their source dump for this device (not all VDFS drivers seem to be able to read all VDFS filesystems), but eventually I had it all extracted, and then I got distracted by other stuff, so let’s fast forward to this week.Samsung makes use of a modified version of the Android Debug Bridge called sdb, which is included in the Tizen SDK. The firmware showed that this device had sdbd on it, and it would be executed if a network device called “huart0” was plugged in. Samsung does, thankfully, provide the source code for their GPLed components, so I could dig through that to discover that drivers/net/usb/usbnet.c had a bunch of references to huart (which apparently stands for “HyperUART”). If CONFIG_SAMSUNG_USBNET_HYPERUART_IFNAME is set, and if the ethernet device is using either the asix or ax88179_178a drivers, and if “/opt/etc/HyperUART_IP_Addr” isn’t just “0”, it sets the interface name to “huart0” and in turn triggers sdbd startup. So now I just needed to figure out how to set /opt/etc/HyperUART_IP_Addr to something else.Some digging revealed a binary called wap-factory that referenced the file, which then led to /usr/share/mobile-mgr/jsons/com.samsung.audio.waapp-verification-test.json which mentioned a “SetUartOnOff” call, which brought me here, which led me into a bit of a rabbit hole about the Samsung WAM protocol. Long story short, you connect to either port 55001 or 56001 and make two requests over the same connection:and then plug in an asix chipset ethernet adapter into the USB port (which on mine is micro-B, so I needed an OTG adapter), and suddenly it’s sitting there on 192.168.250.250 and will speak sdb to you. switches it into root mode, and now gives you a root shell. I was in, and now I could investigate what was happening.First up, there was a process called “com.samsung.audio.google-cast-control-app” running, which seemed like a good start. Unfortunately it wasn’t doing anything. After some tracing I found that it was making a call to Samsung at startup time, and getting back a response telling it that Cast support wasn’t available. The request (which was helpfully dumped to stdout when I ran this by hand) included the country code, in my case “US”. Repeating the request by hand with curl and changing the code to “AU” told me it supported, so now I needed to figure out how to get the soundbar to believe it was Australian. Some digging showed it was reading this from a config variable called db/comss/countrycode, and runninggot me past that gate. Now, however, it was complaining that it couldn’t provision a key. /usr/apps/com.samsung.audio.google-cast-control-app/shared/res included a bunch of encrypted blobs and an app called teeStoreKey.elf, and tracing com.samsung.audio.google-cast-control-app showed it was trying to call that, but it seemed like it was failing with a permissions issue. Running com.samsung.audio.google-cast-control-ap directly as root triggered key provisioning successfully, and a few seconds later the rest of the Cast API came up and I could talk to port 8443 with standard Cast API calls. Unfortunately it still wasn’t working as a Cast device, though - it wasn’t advertising itself via mDNS and so nothing could see it. Querying the /setup/eureka_info endpoint gave me a clue - the ’tos_accepted’ field was false. Normally this would be set as part of initial device setup, but the Samsung app wasn’t doing that because it didn’t think the device had Cast support. It turns out that POSTing some json with {“tos_accepted”: true} to setup/set_eureka_info made it work, and suddenly there was an additional Cast device available to me.(Update: I realised I didn’t mention anything about it was doing key provisioning in the first place! The Cast protocol doesn’t enforce cryptographic identity as such, but Google’s reference client implementation which is what almost everything uses verifies that the device is presenting an identity that chains back to Google. Unsurprisingly they don’t want the private key material to be easily extractable and used to produce clone devices, so it’s all supposed to be encrypted and only accessible to some sort of trusted execution environment, which is why keys here need to be loaded into Trustzone and never be visible in the clear to the main OS)Mission accomplished. Unfortunately the device vanished from my Smartthings home aferwards, presumably because there’s a mismatch between its reported country code and my account country. To get around that I’d somehow need to get com.samsung.audio.google-cast-control-app to either change the query without changing the global device country, or to ignore the response from Samsung (it does this every 24 hours, ugh), and that’s made more annoying by the fact that this thing will only execute signed binaries. Although, weirdly, one of the signed binaries shipped is a full Python interpreter, so if I cared enough I could probably cobble together enough Python to execute arbitrary binaries. I currently don’t.More modern soundbars don’t implement the listener on port 55001 or 56001. I don’t know how you get sdb working on them.

item.title: I often find typos cognitively fascinating.
item.content:encoded: I often find typos cognitively fascinating.Some typos are just last-moment motor errors: "aimed for this key and hit the one next to it". Those are easy to understand. But others reveal much more interesting things about the mental process of driving your fingers on the keyboard, or even composing words.I once aimed to type 'programs', and unexpectedly 'rpgroasm' came out. All the left-hand letters appear in the correct order, and so do all the right-hand letters, but they're interleaved in a spectacularly wrong way. That suggested that one part of my brain had sent an independent set of instructions to a subthing controlling each hand, and everything worked fine except the synchronisation between the two subthings.There's another class of typo which I think of as 'brain got ahead of fingers': you're typing one word, but already thinking about a word that will come after it, and there's a crossover and you end up mixing up the two. Like 'bit bisect' in place of 'git bisect' – you're already planning the b, and it comes out of your fingers prematurely.(Appropriately, as I typed _that_ sentence, 'in place' came out as 'pl inace', wow.)Even the 'boring' motor errors have something cognitively interesting about them, just on the reading rather than writing side. We see 'adjacent letter on the keyboard' typos a lot, so our brains get good at correcting them. Sometimes _over_-correcting, so that you imagine a typo where none existed. When a sentence is a bit unexpected in context, I've been known to consider the possibility of a typo before figuring out how the sentence as originally spelled makes sense.The best ones of those are when I hadn't even _realised_ the two words were a typo apart. I misread 'auction' as 'suction' once and it was a total surprise!I wonder if there's any serious scholarly study of this kind of thing.
