item.title: Russell Coker: Fuel Should be More Expensive
item.author: etbe
item.content:encoded: Before the US and Israel started attacking Iran at the end of February the petrol prices in Australia were around $1.70/L, which for American readers is roughly equivalent to $US4.64/Gal. By the 11th of March the prices were around $2.19/L. Over the same time period Diesel went from around $1.77/L to $2.40/L. The 11th of March prices weren’t necessarily unreasonable prices. In mid March it was reasonable to expect that the US would stop doing such ridiculously stupid things and make a deal with Iran to allow oil to be transported.But every time you think there’s a limit to Trump’s stupidity (and the incompetence of people around him who don’t point him in the right direction) they do something worse. So now we have the Strait of Hormuz almost entirely closed cutting off oil from Kuwait, Qatar, and UAE. The Bab al-Mandab Strait is closed to Saudi linked ships and the Saudi East-West pipeline is closed so once the Yanbu storage tanks are empty there won’t be much if any oil from Saudi Arabia for some time. So world oil supplies will be significantly reduced for a long time.Currently the petrol prices in Melbourne are around $2.30/L and Diesel prices around $2.70/L, not much more expensive than it was in March in spite of all the extra problems both militarily and diplomatically since then. Those prices have been steady for over a month.The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz could be ended fairly quickly and there are reports that a lot of the oil that used to go through it is being re-routed. The damaged infrastructure throughout the middle east can’t be fixed in a hurry. The Bab al-Mandab Strait probably can’t be opened quickly as the Houthis probably don’t have a centralised command structure that allows someone to order a ceasefire and have it stick. So we can expect a massive reduction in world oil supplies for a while, which given the way the US is going could be at least until after the mid-term elections (November this year) and possibly until after the 2028 elections. After that oil production will be reduced for another year or two to rebuild infrastructure.When supply can’t meet demand there are three options. Supply can be rationed, demand can be decreased by increasing the prices, or it can be used up and we run out. Running out of fuel is a really bad option as fuel is needed for producing and transporting food and for most things that are important to a society.Governments of first world countries seem unable to deal with the situation properly. Dealing with it properly requires either rationing or increasing the prices. Instead governments have been more interested in artificially keeping the prices down.Currently in Australia and most countries a significant portion of public transport depends on Diesel fuel. Diesel is needed for most buses and for long distance trains. Most taxis run on petrol. As far as I know all emergency service vehicles run on Diesel or petrol as well as most military vehicles. So things will get really bad quickly if fuel runs out entirely. It’s not just personal cars that are affected.We aren’t going to get the majority of tractors converted to electric power any time soon. Google search results suggest that tractors last an average of about 25 years but casual observation of working equipment on farms suggests a longer life than that is common. Some tractors could be retrofitted to be electric but many will end up being scrapped as part of a conversion while farmers are already having financial problems. It would probably be optimistic to expect that half the tractor use could be done with electric tractors in 10 years time unless there are significant government subsidies. To get the farming and food production industries adapted for electric operation in a few years would be possible but it would take a level of national mobilisation that only happens during wartime.As a long term solution we need to have more electric vehicles in every category. We need electricity for all train lines to replace Diesel locomotives. We need better trains between cities to reduce the need for aeroplanes, electric aeroplanes are being developed but we aren’t there yet. We need all essential services to be run with electric vehicles including farming, food transport, emergency services, and everything related to the medical system (including personal cars for healthcare workers). We also need mining vehicles powered by electricity so we can have the entire industrial system running without fuel. None of this is going to happen in time for this crisis.Electric buses are being introduced in Australia and many taxis are electric. The recent significant increase in the use of electric cars probably includes a reasonable portion of healthcare workers and other essential workers. This gives us the potential to survive fairly severe reductions in the fuel supply without everything collapsing. But we have a significant lack in electric police cars and in electric trucks for food delivery.In the short term we need to significantly reduce the use of fuels, there is no other way to keep the food supply and other essential parts of society working. We could try rationing but I think that should be a last resort. The news reports of a de-facto petrol rationing system in Crimea and parts of Russia are not positive, significant resources are wasted in long queues for petrol and there is public disorder caused by disputes about position in the queues. The level of sanity in the population seems to have dropped significantly since the fuel crisis of 1979, any fuel rationing that is implemented now would get the same sort of opposition from Qanon types as Covid vaccines and lockdowns did in recent times.So the best viable option seems to be to reduce demand by increasing prices. $2.30/L as a common price with occasional spikes of $2.50/L isn’t sufficient to do that. If the price increased to $3.50/L, twice what it used to be (equivalent to $9.50/gallon for Americans) then it would provide a real incentive for people to reduce fuel use. That would have to be combined with the type of remote work allowances that were in place when Covid19 was first spreading. But I think that all politicians are too weak to do such things. The media have demonstrated that nowadays the best we can expect is that they will treat both sides as equal even when facts clearly support one side, so we can’t expect the media to report on impending fuel shortages and demand policy changes to address them.We should have higher taxes on fuel that will continue past the resolution of the current crisis caused by the attacks on Iran to provide incentives for the purchase of electric cars and for manufacturers to make more fuel efficient cars. Currently people are basing car ownership decisions on the expectation that petrol will go back to something under $2/L and we need to have a government guarantee that it won’t happen.People always complain about poor people who can’t afford to drive if petrol is expensive but that could be addressed by increasing the minimum wage and social security payments. But a large portion of the people who complain about the hardship poor people may face when fuel prices are discussed are against increasing the minimum wage so I don’t think they are being honest.Another common complaint is about the difficulty driving long distances in rural Australia when there isn’t sufficient charging infrastructure for electric cars and therefore rural people including farmers getting hit by high prices of fuel. There could be a rebate scheme for farmers etc, government subsidies for farmers is nothing new.I expect the governments of most first world countries to try to keep fuel prices low and do very little to try and decrease demand. China will probably do some things to reduce fuel use and being the world’s largest oil importer this will make a difference, but not as much as we need.A related problem is that a lot of fertiliser is produced from petrochemicals and closing the strait of Hormuz cut off a significant portion of the world fertiliser supply. First world countries will outbid developing countries for fertiliser and fuel. Starvation in developing countries probably won’t get much news coverage until it leads to war.This is not going to go well, it could be addressed if we had braver politicians and more honest media companies but that’s not the way things are going.

item.title: Russell Coker: Radxa Rock 5A RK3588S
item.author: etbe
item.content:encoded: At the end of last year I paid $177.40 for a Radxa ROCK 5A GREEN RK3588S, 8-core CPU SBC, HDMI with 8K Output, WiFi 6 Support and Gigabit Ethernet, Single Board Computer [1] from AliExpress. I got the version with 8G of RAM as 4G didn’t seem enough and I didn’t feel like paying for the 16G or 32G versions. The prices excluding postage are $106, $130, $203, and $332 for the 4G, 8G, 16G, and 32G versions respectively. The $332 version is quite reasonably priced if you need to do some big compiles on ARM64. Since then the prices have changed by a few dollars but are almost the same (variations in postage will be greater than the price changes).I installed Bookworm and upgraded it to Trixie (the current Debian release). There were some conflicts with some radxa packages that contained the same files as Trixie packages but didn’t have a package conflict but it was not a big deal. It would be nice if Radxa updated their setup to Trixie and it wouldn’t be that difficult for them to do so.The board has an expansion bus which apparently can be used for NVMe. It also has an option for a EMMC module. But if you get the default configuration then the only boot device supported is a micro SD card.The next thing I considered doing is running it for playing movies on a 4K but it turns out to not support HDMI audio (at least not with the supplied drivers) and has no other audio support. Apparently boards like this have a common use case of digital signs where audio isn’t required.I had this post in draft for a year because I planned to write more, but I haven’t come up with anything. It’s not an exciting device. Handy to have another ARM test and build system and handy to be able to test high resolution video with a portable device but I don’t use it for much. I guess “just works in a boring way” isn’t a bad review.

item.title: I had a really good afternoon at work yesterday.
item.content:encoded: I had a really good afternoon at work yesterday.I had a long pair-debugging session with a junior colleague, helping to track down a crash in something they were in the middle of writing. We started from the visible crash and backtracked to find the root cause, investigating everything along the way that looked odd.We were expecting one bug, but ended up finding two. The load instruction that first put a bogus value into a register was loading from a totally wrong address, *and* there was some weird data at that address that shouldn't have been there, and those two wrong things had independent causes.Neither bug by itself would have caused the crash: it needed both. If we'd found only one of them – for example by jumping to a conclusion, speculatively fixing something, and observing that the crash had gone away – then we'd have thought the whole problem was fixed, and been wrong. But by going through methodically to the point where the first weird thing happened, we were able to find both bugs. We fixed one on the spot, and ended the session knowing what to do about the other.My colleague had asked for help with the aim of learning debugging skills (both low-level and general) as well as getting the bug fixed. I don't always have success when I do this on real-world problems, because if the problem turns out to be too hard, I can't solve it _and_ explain what I'm doing at the same time. Here, it was just about right: challenging, but not too much so.I learned things too. We had to use LLDB rather than GDB, and I'm not nearly as familiar with LLDB, and now I'm more so. (It has a proper hex-dump command!) So it was a useful learning experience on both sides, as well as a successful bug-fixing exercise. They apologised afterwards for taking up my whole afternoon, but I think it was time well spent.And to put the icing on the cake, nobody at any point suggested throwing an LLM at anything.The only thing that bothers me about it is that this kind of experience is now rare enough in my life that I feel moved to toot about it when it happens!

item.title: Enrico Zini: Sandboxing pre-commit
item.author: Enrico Zini
item.content:encoded: pre-commit is a tool that is often a prerequisite for contributing to Python upstream projects. It installs as a git pre-commit hook and runs various checks on commit, using tools installed in a set of virtualenvs that it automatically manages.In other words, it is a Remote Code Execution engine running with the permissions of your own user, and with read and write access to all your information (including, say, or ). If you are lucky, and for as long as you're lucky, it will perform useful tasks on your code.However, I didn't want to end up with another containerized OS tree that it's then my responsibility to manage, and I tried to go the bubblewrap way, so that the environment where runs will get the same security updates as the rest of my system.Runs in a private filesystem, with no access to user's files or system configurationRuns in a filesystem where everything is read-only, except for the git working directoryEven the directory is readonly, so that changes in the code can be reliably detected via Runs without network unless explicitly requested by the userHere's a breakdown of the options I used so far.Set up usual filesystem expectations: --ro-bind /usr /usr \ --symlink usr/bin /bin \ --symlink usr/lib64 /lib64 \ --symlink usr/lib /lib \ --proc /proc \ --dev /dev \ Make the working directory and pre-commit's environments storage available and writable: --bind ${CURDIR} "$GUEST_DIR" \ --bind ~/.cache/pre-commit "/home/${USER}/.cache/pre-commit" \ --chdir "$GUEST_DIR" \ Forward git's configuration: --ro-bind /etc/gitconfig /etc/gitconfig \ --ro-bind ~/.gitconfig /home/${USER}/.gitconfig \ Make writable (pre-commit needs to stash, for example), but use a tmpfs overlay so that the writes don't persist: --overlay-src "$CURDIR/.git" \ --tmp-overlay "$GUEST_DIR/.git" \ Remove access to everything except the above. Prevent keystroke injection at the terminal. Propagate . --unshare-all \ --new-session \ --die-with-parent --share-net \ --ro-bind /etc/resolv.conf /etc/resolv.conf \ --ro-bind /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt To run it, you can set up the wrapper script to run with a higher priority in , but you need to edit to remove the first branch of the that, frustratingly, tries to run it as .I'm looking forward to a time where it becomes stadard practice to manage user commands this way: why should a desktop solitaire game have access to ? Or network? Why is it still normal, in 2026, to run a Desktop system like that?

Russell Coker: CEO Impersonation Fraud
item.author: etbe
item.content:encoded: CEO fraud (or more generally executive fraud) is a subset of Business Email Compromise fraud which allegedly loses Australian businesses $84M/year [3]. The numbers vary a lot depending on what is counted, is it just attacks where money is lost or do situations where the bank reverses the transaction count? There’s a lot of secrecy around this because of reputation issues related to fraud, a company that gets defrauded might be regarded as an unreliable business partner. Also in terms of interpreting results there are organisations that want to promote the idea that “it’s a major crime that could cost you everything unless you pay us to improve your security”.My experience of these things is that at one company I worked for someone had gained access to an executive mailbox and setup rules to move mail from certain senders to a mailbox that wouldn’t be checked (maybe .Sent or .Spam or something – I can’t remember the details) as well as forwarding it to an address the attacker controlled. That meant that the executive wouldn’t see email from the scam targets while the email gets forwarded to the attackers. At the time it appeared that Office 365 didn’t have any features for sending automatic audit alerts for such changes. I think that all changes to executive email accounts should trigger alerts to the corporate security team (in that case me). One would hope that such exploitation would be a major wake-up call for the company but it wasn’t. It was never discovered how the attacker got access to the account, I presume it was by compromising a personal computer of the executive which they used for company purposes. Having a strong separation of hardware used for work and hardware for personal use is a really good thing.At the same company every time the CEO went on a scheduled trip there would be email sent impersonating him claiming that money needed to be transferred. It was never discovered how the attackers knew when he was on a trip. Was the CEO telling people on LinkedIn about his plans or something? Was his calendar shared to someone outside the company? Was there an employee leaking information? We never found out and surprisingly the executive team didn’t think this was a problem. It’s not necessarily bad for the CEO to publicise their trips even if that alerts hostile parties, but everyone needs to know what the situation is. An unexplained attack is more concerning than a known attack that can be predicted and dealt with.The role of CEO has a unique combination of being able to authorise funds transfers while also being able to reject other security methods. You can tell a line manager that they need to follow the process for a $10 purchase but you can’t necessarily tell the CEO that they need to follow the process for $100,000. Even if the CEO always follows the process for funds transfers you have to convince all the people involved in funds transfers that the CEO will follow the process and any unexpected email demanding an immediate transfer should be rejected.A final problem is getting executives to understand the importance of computer security. My experience is that getting a CTO to adhere to good security practices can be a challenge and that even on the rare occasions someone like me gets to communicate with the CEO it’s not possible to convince them to change anything.Most computer security problems end up as people problems.

item.title: Otto Kekäläinen: Debcraft v1.0 released: Easy, fast and secure way to build Debian packages
item.author: Otto Kekäläinen
item.content:encoded: Debcraft is a tool that automates most of the repetitive and error-prone steps related to Debian packaging. It makes it easy to build packages from source without having to manually prepare build environments. It clearly shows what changed in the build artifacts between two builds, automates parts of importing new upstream versions, and can automatically apply repetitive fixes to the packaging source code, including committing them in git.While doing all of this, it also explains what it does and helps users learn best practices in Debian packaging, making the overall experience much easier and more fun than with any other tool before, while also being secure and fast.Try out Debcraft 1.0 now! Debcraft can be installed simply by running on a recent version of Debian or Ubuntu. Check with that you have . The latest version can also always be installed from source at salsa.debian.org/debian/debcraft (does not require compiling anything).Debcraft was designed to offer the following three main benefits:Build any Debian/Ubuntu package by simply running in the checked-out Debian packaging git repository.If the orig upstream source code tarball is neither already present nor available on a branch, the exact upstream tarball is downloaded from the Debian archive.Users are spared from having to manually prepare ahead or maintain build environments. Debcraft builds create a container on-the-fly (both Podman and Docker supported), built using the target Debian or Ubuntu suite in and with exact build dependencies from .Commands , and automate recurring package maintenance tasks and help maintainers produce high-quality, up-to-date packages, run Salsa CI, pass autopkgtest in Debian CI, and stay in sync across Debian archives and packaging git repositories.The command output is (relatively) easy to read, and it also teaches users about Debian packaging .Container layer caching is utilized to make builds blazingly fast.If an apt-cacher-ng instance or equivalent is present, it will automatically be used.The build phase happens inside hermetic containers with no network access. This ensures all dependencies are properly managed and that the built binaries are as trustworthy as the source code they were built from.Using containers also protects the host system from getting polluted with extra development libraries, and adds an extra layer of protection to prevent anything malicious in the source code from accessing secrets on the host system.The additional logs provided by Debcraft also help audit changes in Debian package sources and build artifacts.Result of many years of development The first commit in the git repository is from 2020 under the name . The project was renamed to Debcraft in a commit on December 8th, 2023. I have been developing this tool fairly actively since 2024 and using it for all my packaging, “dogfooding” so to say.Now, in October 2026, it was time to release Debcraft v1.0 as it has had extensive real-world use and iteration based on countless different packages and multiple users. Users have included both experienced fellow Debian Developers and lots of people who just started learning how Debian packaging works. As I mentor dozens of new contributors to Debian, I have seen that the latter group seems to benefit the most from Debcraft and its ease of use and built-in guidance, while to the more experienced developers the main benefit is having less details to remember and doing less mistakes.The code is intentionally written entirely in shell script to keep the barrier to code contribution as low as possible. It is also very easy to debug, as any command can be run with to emit step-by-step information about what it is doing, and being Bash scripts, injecting anywhere in the code will emit an even more detailed trace of every subcommand executed. if you aspire to become a Debian Developer, and want to follow my examples in using state-of-the-art tooling and collaborate using salsa.debian.org, feel free to reach out for mentorship. I am glad to see more people contribute to Debian!

Amin Bandali: Living healthier
item.author: Amin Bandali
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week I had a coaching session with Protesilaos, where we focused on health and wellness. I took some notes during our call, which I expand on here, and share with Prot's permission. I've been paying more serious attention to my health this year, and our discussion was in the context of me striving to live a healthier life. These notes are shared in the hope of being useful and professional advice; for medical advice please consult a licensed physician.Life in today's fast-paced world can feel busier than ever, where every day is packed with a myriad of activities and tasks that need to be done, or tempting distractions that pop up seemingly randomly, with hardly a moment to spare. Despite that, or perhaps of that, it's worthwhile to make time for ourselves and the various aspects of our health.
As embodied souls, our bodies condition our minds. We take care of our body so we can take care of our mind. As humans we evolved for an active lifestyle out of survival necessity. In today's society many of us have sedentary office jobs that involve sitting for long periods of time. It's especially important that we try and make time for some regular physical activity like exercising and resistance training, to help build and retain muscle mass and mobility as we age. Fitness does not have to be the end goal that takes over our life, though there is nothing wrong with that if fitness one's central goal e.g. as a personal trainer. Rather, for someone like me with other primary goals, my reason to exercise is to help live a healthier life, so I could spend quality time with my loved ones and carry out my responsibilities with a healthy body and mind.Prot mentioned that our health is directly dependent on the following four factors:Thus compromising any of these - for example, eating greasy food or drinking alcohol - would undermine the gains from exercising.While pursuing fitness, it's important to have effort so that the body remains active and the mind is not distracted, and equally important to have effort so that we don't suffer injuries and not make the pursuit of fitness burdensome financially.Calisthenics is a key part of the strength training activities Prot practices, in addition to the physically intensive work he does on his land.Calisthenics [...] is a form of strength training that utilizes an individual's body weight as resistance to perform multi-joint, compound movements with little or no equipment. Calisthenics are popular for their convenience, as they require little to no equipment and can be performed anywhere.Calisthenics can be done progressively, starting small and building in intensity and duration over time. It is also economically/financially sustainable. These calisthenic exercises are a good starting point (barring existing injuries in the related areas):push-ups - easier version: at an angle or against the wall;pull-ups - easier version: at an angle e.g. using door frame;squats - easier version: don't squat all the way down; andAim to perform each exercise in 3 sets of 10 repetitions, but it's perfectly okay to start with fewer and gradually build up. The exercises should be done around the same time everyday, so that there is enough time for the muscles to rest and recover for the next day. Doing them at night then again the next morning, for instance, would be too short of a time period and not enough for the body to recover. It's also vital to get enough sleep each night to make sure the body can properly rest and be energized the next day.As mentioned earlier, it's crucial to pair exercise with a healthy diet. I found Prot's programming metaphor for food interesting: similar to how it takes more time and effort for us to process and understand complex source code, breaking down and processing complex foods is similarly more difficult for the body. Prot does not eat fried food, and recommends avoiding sauces as much as possible: greasy, salty, and creamy extras make food more irresistible. They tend to make one want to eat more than what the body needs, and are to be avoided in isolation but especially in combination. In keeping ingredients close to their natural states, not overdoing things, and not eating more than the body needs, Prot extends his philosophy of simplicity and moderation to cooking.In addition to eating healthy meals, we need to apply similar consideration to snacks: avoiding overly salty or sugary snacks, and choosing healthier ones. Nuts can make great snacks in small quantities, especially almonds and walnuts, if one's not allergic.In addition to the inherent healthiness of the food or snack, Prot also suggests paying attention to methods of preparation. For instance, regarding concentration or distillation: juices, even when freshly squeezed from fruits, might have more of the fruits' sugar than its pulp and other beneficial parts. Additionally, chewing triggers biological responses in our body which for example can reduce stress, and release satiety hormones to help avoid overeating. So, Prot suggests to just eat the fruits themselves.Regarding weight loss, it will occur naturally as we introduce exercise into our routine, and pay closer attention to what we eat and drink. It's important to lose the weight slowly to condition our body to the new reality as it changes. Shortcuts tend to either not work, or have negative consequences. By going through the process slowly and with regularity, we gradually retrain our muscle memories and adjust our habits so we can maintain the lower weight and the healthier lifestyle. Regularity is key: it's better do a little everyday, than do a lot on only two days. It helps us develop the attitude that the exercise is part of our regular effort that we do consistently all the time.Working on wellness and living healthier is a matter of moderation, and building capacity over time. I will give it the time and attention it needs, without rushing, and enjoy the journey to becoming a healthier version of myself.Take care, and so long for now.

item.title: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo: Restricting device memory usage on Linux 7.3
item.author: Thadeu Lima de Souza Cascardo
item.content:encoded: Linux cgroups has been used for a while to group processes and control their access to certain system resources. One of those resources is memory, through the use of memcg. That control is dynamic, allowing for cgroups to setup a minimal and a maximal amount of memory, as well as low and high thresholds, which will control the reclaim process.But what about device memory that is not available as system RAM? Memory that is not available to the Linux page allocator? One of those device memories is GPU VRAM.That's where the dmem cgroup controller comes in. Introduced in Linux 6.14, it was first adopted by the Intel Xe driver. In Linux 6.15, AMD amdgpu driver also adopted it. In 7.3, it was adopted by nouveau.Such a cgroup controller allows the system to be configured such that a workload, be it a browser, a game, or another GPU rendering process can have some minimal VRAM available. Or it can prevent one of these processes from using all VRAM, preventing your compositor from using it, for example.Let's go through the system knobs that are available to control this and what's new in Linux 7.3.dmem regions and dmem.capacitySince a given system might have multiple GPUs, there might be multiple device memory regions. So, on dmem, each such region is described by a name. Every dmem cgroup setting file will contain one line per region. One of those files shows the capacity of each region in bytes and is present only in the root cgroup.After enabling the dmem cgroup with the following command:# echo +dmem > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control One can inspect the capacity of any available regions by looking at at the root cgroup:# cat /sys/fs/cgroup/dmem.capacity drm/0000:03:00.0/vram 8573157376 That shows that the GPU at PCI address 0000:03:00.0 has a 8176MiB VRAM dmem region.When introduced at 6.14, the following settings were available.In every dmem cgroup, including the root cgroup, the dmem.current is a read-only file that shows the current usage of each region by the given cgroup.# cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/dmem.current drm/0000:03:00.0/vram 292757504 Here, it shows that user.slice cgroup is currently using above 292 MB of VRAM.# cat /sys/fs/cgroup/dmem.current drm/0000:03:00.0/vram 311377920 Here, we can check that total system usage is above 311 MB.Excluding the root cgroup, dmem cgroups can control the maximal number of bytes that can be allocated from a region by processes in that cgroup. If an allocation moves the usage above the max setting, it will be refused. In that case, the allocation might be attempted at system memory or it might trigger eviction, depending on the allocation parameters and the driver.Here, the value has special meaning, which is unrestricted usage.# echo drm/0000:03:00.0/vram 536870912 > /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/dmem.max # cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/dmem.max drm/0000:03:00.0/vram 536870912 # echo drm/0000:03:00.0/vram max > /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/dmem.max # cat /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/dmem.max drm/0000:03:00.0/vram max dmem.min, also not available on the root cgroup, will control the eviction process - when memory needs to be moved out of VRAM to make room for other VRAM allocations. If an object belongs to a cgroup which is using less than its min setting, it will not be considered for eviction. It effectively works as a hard protection such that the cgroup can use at least the minimal setting.Given multiple cgroups may set a minimal value that exceeds the device memory capacity, it computes an effective minimal depending on the hierarchy.While dmem.min works as a hard limit, dmem.low is a soft limit that will prevent eviction in case other objects from different cgroups are available for eviction. That is, the system will try to evict from different, possibly unprotected cgroups, before it tries to evict from a cgroup if evicting would leave its usage below the value set as dmem.low.Recent developments in Linux 7.3Some new changes have been recently introduced in the dmem cgroup controller and its integration with GPUs.One of those is a new read-only file, , which was introduced to allow the peak usage of a region in a cgroup to be inspected.Also, Linux 7.3 fixed certain scenarios where a given cgroup would not be able to allocate VRAM up to its minimal or low limits if other processes had already allocated most of VRAM, even though they had no such limits set.Changing multiple regions' settings in a single write was possible before 7.3, but it was prone to failures which would not be reported to userspace and might have left the values partially updated. Starting with 7.3, only one region may be updated per write.And, finally, prior to 7.3, setting in a cgroup that was using more than the new setting would silently fail. Now, there is a mechanism that allows a reclaim mechanism to be triggered. That way, when a process writes to and sets a maximal value below the current usage, it will wait (unless is used) for the reclaim process to move objects out of VRAM until the usage gets below the maximal value. If that is not possible for some reason, the setting will still be in place, restricting further alloctions by that cgroup.

item.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: RcppArmadillo 15.6.2-1 on CRAN: New Upstream
item.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
item.content:encoded: Armadillo is a powerful and expressive C++ template library for linear algebra and scientific computing. It aims towards a good balance between speed and ease of use, has a syntax deliberately close to Matlab, and is useful for algorithm development directly in C++, or quick conversion of research code into production environments. RcppArmadillo integrates this library with the R environment and language–and is widely used by (currently) 1370 other packages on CRAN, downloaded 49.4 million times (per the partial logs from the cloud mirrors of CRAN), and the CSDA paper (preprint / vignette) by Conrad and myself has been cited 735 times according to Google Scholar.This versions updates to the 15.6.2 upstream Armadillo release made yesterday. It, along with 15.6.1 release we incorporated earlier, addresses only minor issues and should not present any user-facing changes. As usual, we did run full reverse-depdency checks against the over 1300 ackages, and did not find anything. As usual, we aim to accommodate the desired CRAN cadences for uploads and try not to exceed six in six months—so we did not ship 15.6.1-1 there. The package has also already been updated for Debian, built for r2u and r-universe, and will build shortly at CRAN for the different binary releases.All changes since the last CRAN release follow.Changes in RcppArmadillo version 15.6.2-1 (2026-10-16)Upgraded to Armadillo release 15.6.2 (Medium Roast Cortado)Faster inplace addition of expressionsChanges in RcppArmadillo version 15.6.1-1 [github-only] (2026-10-02)Upgraded to Armadillo release 15.6.1 (Medium Roast Cortado)Fix for failures in when using the (non-default) "std" method

item.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: RcppSimdJson 0.1.17 on CRAN: Updates
item.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
item.content:encoded: RcppSimdJson wraps the fantastic and genuinely impressive simdjson library by Daniel Lemire and collaborators. Via very clever algorithmic engineering to obtain largely branch-free code, coupled with modern C++ and newer compiler instructions, it results in parsing gigabytes of JSON parsed per second which is quite mindboggling. The best-case performance is ‘faster than CPU speed’ as use of parallel SIMD instructions and careful branch avoidance can lead to less than one cpu cycle per byte parsed; see the video of the talk by Daniel Lemire at QCon.This release is a small increment relative to the 0.1.6 release last week that got us (upstream) version 5.0.2 with many notable changes and sizeable speed gains on all fronts, including the interface from R. However, this failed to compile at CRAN on macOS x86_64 as the machine is setup for only partial support of C++20: no ranges, no concepts. So we now test, and fall back to C++17 if the test compilation fails. Upstream, meanwhile, already got to 5.0.5 which is included. It also gets us improved handling of disabling pragmas which we hope will survive CRAN checks.The brief NEWS entry for this release follows.Changes in version 0.1.17 [unreleased] (2026-10-xx)Compilation starts with a C++20 feature test; if this fails C++17 is used (Dirk in #111 fixing #110) was upgraded to version 5.0.5 (Daniel in #112)

item.title: Got lucky with a web search just now.
item.content:encoded: Got lucky with a web search just now.I wanted to debug a crash in LLVM. For other programs I'd start by compiling with Address Sanitizer. LLVM's build process is tricky enough that you might not do that the obvious way, so I websearched "build llvm with address sanitizer".Foolish me! That can also be interpreted as "build an LLVM toolchain that includes ASan for end users to use on the programs they build with it". Most of the hits were about that, and not about the thing I wanted.But lucky me! I found a Stack Overflow post that recognised the ambiguity and answered _both_ questions. Top marks, that poster.(The answer is "-DLLVM_USE_SANITIZER=Address".)
